scenes.head: Inflation and real returns
scenes.sub: A dollar next year is not the same unit as a dollar today. Measure inflation over several years, convert amounts into today’s dollars, use the exact Fisher relation, and discount nominal cash flows at nominal rates and real cash flows at real rates, so that every comparison across time is made in one kind of dollar.

segs.say: Inflation and real returns. A dollar next year is not the same unit as a dollar today. Measure inflation over several years, convert amounts into today’s dollars, use the exact Fisher relation, and discount nominal cash flows at nominal rates and real cash flows at real rates, so that every comparison across time is made in one kind of dollar.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Calculate yearly, cumulative and average annual inflation from a price index over several years.
Convert a nominal amount at any date into real dollars of a chosen base date, and back again.
Apply the exact Fisher relation to find a real rate, a nominal rate or an inflation rate, using effective rates for the same period.
Calculate the present value of a cash-flow stream both in nominal terms and in real terms, and explain why consistent discounting gives the same answer.
Calculate the real growth of a salary or a price, and explain how Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) keep their purchasing power.

scenes.head: March 2027.

segs.say: March 2027. Lantern Coffee Co. is a year old, and a law firm in the city (fictional, like everything in the case) wants Lantern to cater its staff events and client meetings for three years. It offers two ways to pay, each fee paid at the end of each contract year: a fixed $42,000 a year, or $40,000 a year in March 2027 dollars, raised every year in line with the Consumer Price Index. Ana still assumes, as she did in F00, that prices will rise by about 2.8% a year, and she wants Lantern’s contracts to earn 10% a year, the return she judges fair for the risk of the business. The indexed fee starts lower but grows. Which is worth more today? Answering means comparing dollars paid in different years when each year’s dollar buys a little less than the last.

scenes.head: In F00 you met inflation as a sustained rise in prices and saw that it reduces the purchasing power of money.

segs.say: In F00 you met inflation as a sustained rise in prices and saw that it reduces the purchasing power of money. Over one year that was a single division. Over several years, and with cash flowing in and out at different dates, it pays to be explicit about which kind of dollar each number is measured in.

Nominal amount. An amount in the dollars of the date it is actually paid or received: the number on the cheque. Also called current dollars. Prices, wages, loan payments and bank balances are all quoted in nominal terms.

Real amount. The same amount restated in the purchasing power of a chosen base period, by dividing out the inflation between the base and the date of payment. Also called constant dollars, or “today’s dollars” when the base is today.

scenes.head: A real amount answers the question “what would this buy at base-period prices?” Lantern’s indexed fee is set in real terms: $40,000 of March 2027…

segs.say: A real amount answers the question “what would this buy at base-period prices?” Lantern’s indexed fee is set in real terms: $40,000 of March 2027 purchasing power every year. The fixed fee is set in nominal terms: $42,000 in each year’s dollars, which buy less as time passes. Neither form is wrong; mixing them without converting is.

scenes.head: A price index such as the Consumer Price Index measures the cost of a fixed basket relative to a base period.

segs.say: A price index such as the Consumer Price Index measures the cost of a fixed basket relative to a base period. The table follows a fictional index for five years. Each year’s inflation is the percentage change in the index over that year, exactly as in F00.
A fictional price index over five years (Year 0 = 100)

scenes.head: Two summary numbers matter.

segs.say: Two summary numbers matter. Cumulative inflation is the total rise: 122.9 ÷ 100.0 − 1 = 22.9%. The average annual inflation rate is the constant yearly rate that would have produced the same total, so it is found by compounding backwards, not by dividing: (122.9 ÷ 100.0)^(1/5) − 1 ≈ 4.21%. Check it: 1.042102⁵ ≈ 1.229. Dividing the cumulative figure by five gives 4.58%, which is too high, because it ignores the fact that each year’s inflation applies to prices that have already risen.

scenes.head: Yearly rates link by multiplication, never by addition: 1.032 × 1.0630 × 1.0611 × 1.0275 × 1.0276 ≈ 1.229, the same ratio as the end and start index…

segs.say: Yearly rates link by multiplication, never by addition: 1.032 × 1.0630 × 1.0611 × 1.0275 × 1.0276 ≈ 1.229, the same ratio as the end and start index levels. This is the compound-growth arithmetic of module 1 applied to prices.

chapters.title: Restating amounts in one kind of dollar

scenes.head: To restate a nominal amount paid at date t in dollars of a base date, multiply by the ratio of the index at the base to the index at t.

segs.say: To restate a nominal amount paid at date t in dollars of a base date, multiply by the ratio of the index at the base to the index at t. Suppose a fictional technician earned $45,000 in Year 0 and $52,000 in Year 5 on the index above. In Year 0 dollars, the Year 5 salary is 52,000 × 100.0 ÷ 122.9 ≈ 42,310.82 dollars. Her pay rose 15.56% in dollars, but in purchasing power it fell about 5.98%. To have kept pace with prices she would have needed 45,000 × 1.229 = 55,305 dollars in Year 5.

scenes.head: The same ratio works in either direction, and the base can be any date: today, the start of a contract, or a year you want to compare against.

segs.say: The same ratio works in either direction, and the base can be any date: today, the start of a contract, or a year you want to compare against. What matters is that every amount in one calculation is measured against the same base.

chapters.title: Nominal rates, real rates and the Fisher relation

scenes.head: F00 gave the exact link between a nominal return, inflation i and a real return.

segs.say: F00 gave the exact link between a nominal return, inflation i and a real return. This course calls it the Fisher relation: 1 + rₙₒₘ = (1 + rᵣₑₐₗ)(1 + i). It can be solved for whichever rate is unknown. Ana wants Lantern’s contracts to earn 10% a year in nominal terms; with 2.8% inflation that is a real return of 1.10 ÷ 1.028 − 1 ≈ 7.00%. Run the other way, an investor who wants 7% real when inflation is 2.8% needs 1.07 × 1.028 − 1 ≈ 10.00% nominal.

scenes.head: Discount like with like

segs.say: Discount like with like. Nominal cash flows are discounted at a nominal rate; real cash flows are discounted at a real rate. Done consistently, the two routes give exactly the same present value, because inflation is divided out of both the numerator and the denominator. Mixing them, real flows with a nominal rate or nominal flows with a real rate, is one of the most common and most expensive errors in valuation.

scenes.head: For Lantern’s indexed offer, the nominal route grows the fee with expected inflation, 40,000 × 1.028ᵗ in year t, and discounts at 10%.

segs.say: For Lantern’s indexed offer, the nominal route grows the fee with expected inflation, 40,000 × 1.028ᵗ in year t, and discounts at 10%. The real route keeps the fee at $40,000 and discounts at the real rate of about 7.00%. Both give about $104,965.18. The fixed $42,000, already nominal, is worth 42,000 × 2.486852 ≈ 104,447.78 at 10%. On Ana’s inflation assumption the indexed offer is worth about $517.40 more today, and it also protects Lantern if inflation turns out higher. Worked example 2 sets out every step.

scenes.head: Write CPIₜ for the index level at date t.

segs.say: Write CPIₜ for the index level at date t. Inflation over any interval is the ratio of the index levels minus one, however many years the interval spans. Because the ratio over a long interval is the product of the ratios over the shorter intervals inside it, yearly rates compound: (1 + i₁)(1 + i₂)…(1 + iₙ) = CPIₙ ÷ CPI₀. The average annual rate is the nth root of that product minus one, a geometric average, for the same reason that the average growth rate of an investment is.

scenes.head: Monthly figures annualise the same way.

segs.say: Monthly figures annualise the same way. If an index rises 0.3% in a month, the annualised rate is 1.003¹² − 1 ≈ 3.66%, not 12 × 0.3% = 3.6%. Over a full year, the year-on-year change in the index (this month’s level against the same month a year earlier) is usually the more reliable figure, because single months are noisy.

scenes.head: A price index is an average over a basket, so it is a measure, not a law of nature.

segs.say: A price index is an average over a basket, so it is a measure, not a law of nature. The CPI tracks what urban consumers buy; a business’s own costs, such as coffee beans or rent, may rise faster or slower. When a contract is linked to an index, the parties must name the exact series. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics, which publishes the CPI, recommends the US City Average index for escalation clauses and calls seasonally adjusted figures inappropriate for them; seasonally adjusted data are also revised for up to five years after release.

scenes.head: The exact relation 1 + rₙₒₘ = (1 + rᵣₑₐₗ)(1 + i) holds over any period, provided all three rates are measured over the same period and compound in…

segs.say: The exact relation 1 + rₙₒₘ = (1 + rᵣₑₐₗ)(1 + i) holds over any period, provided all three rates are measured over the same period and compound in the same way. Two consequences follow.

Use effective rates. A savings account quoted at 4.5% a year compounded monthly has an effective annual rate of (1 + 0.045/12)¹² − 1 ≈ 4.594%. Its real return at 2.8% inflation is 1.04594 ÷ 1.028 − 1 ≈ 1.745%. Using the quoted 4.5% would give 1.654%, understating the real return by about 0.09 percentage points.

It works over several years. Over n years the growth factors multiply: (1 + rₙₒₘ)ⁿ = (1 + rᵣₑₐₗ)ⁿ (1 + i)ⁿ. The cumulative real return is the cumulative nominal growth divided by cumulative inflation, minus one. Approximating by subtraction each year and adding up the errors can go badly wrong over long horizons, as F00 showed.

scenes.head: The approximation rᵣₑₐₗ ≈ rₙₒₘ − i drops the term rᵣₑₐₗ × i.

segs.say: The approximation rᵣₑₐₗ ≈ rₙₒₘ − i drops the term rᵣₑₐₗ × i. OpenStax’s Principles of Finance presents that subtraction as the working definition of the real interest rate; this course uses the exact form for every calculation and the subtraction only as a mental check.

scenes.head: A cash flow expected in year t can be written either way.

segs.say: A cash flow expected in year t can be written either way. If C^(real)ₜ is its value in today’s dollars and inflation is expected to run at i a year, the nominal amount is C^(nom)ₜ = C^(real)ₜ (1 + i)ᵗ. Discounting each at its matching rate gives the same present value, term by term:
(C^(nom)ₜ)/(1 + rₙₒₘ)ᵗ = (C^(real)ₜ (1 + i)ᵗ)/((1 + rᵣₑₐₗ)ᵗ (1 + i)ᵗ) = (C^(real)ₜ)/(1 + rᵣₑₐₗ)ᵗ
Lantern’s indexed offer valued both ways (10% nominal, 2.8% inflation, 7.0039% real)

scenes.head: The two inconsistent mixes show how large the error can be.

segs.say: The two inconsistent mixes show how large the error can be. Discounting the real $40,000 at the nominal 10% gives 40,000 × 2.486852 ≈ 99,474.08, about $5,491.10 too low: it treats the fee as if it never rose, while the discount rate still charges for inflation. Discounting the nominal fees at the real 7.00% gives about $110,815.59, about $5,850.41 too high: inflation is counted in the cash flows but not in the rate.

scenes.head: The annuities lesson gives a check.

segs.say: The annuities lesson gives a check. Nominal fees that start at $41,120 and grow at 2.8% form a growing annuity, whose value at 10% is 41,120/(0.10 − 0.028)[1 − (1.028/1.10)³] ≈ 104,965.18: the same answer a third way. A level real payment is the same thing as a nominal payment growing at the inflation rate.

scenes.head: Which route to choose

segs.say: Which route to choose. Use whichever route matches how the cash flows are forecast. Prices quoted “in today’s money”, budgets prepared without inflation and CPI-linked contracts are naturally real; loan payments, bond coupons, fixed-price contracts and anything written as a number of dollars on a date are nominal. A fixed nominal payment must be converted before it can be discounted at a real rate, and the conversion needs an inflation forecast.

chapters.title: Real growth of salaries and prices

scenes.head: The Fisher relation applies to any growth rate, not only to interest.

segs.say: The Fisher relation applies to any growth rate, not only to interest. A salary growing at g a year in nominal terms grows in real terms at gᵣₑₐₗ = (1 + g) ÷ (1 + i) − 1. Suppose Lantern hires a barista trainer on $42,000 with raises of 3.5% a year (a fictional offer). At 2.8% inflation the real raise is 1.035 ÷ 1.028 − 1 ≈ 0.68% a year. After four years the salary is 42,000 × 1.035⁴ ≈ 48,195.97 dollars, which buys what about 48,195.97 ÷ 1.028⁴ ≈ 43,155.71 dollars buys today: a 14.75% rise in dollars, a 2.75% rise in purchasing power.

scenes.head: An ordinary bond promises fixed nominal payments, so its holder bears inflation risk: if inflation is higher than expected, the payments buy less.

segs.say: An ordinary bond promises fixed nominal payments, so its holder bears inflation risk: if inflation is higher than expected, the payments buy less. An inflation-protected bond moves that risk to the issuer by indexing the principal. In the United States the best known are Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), issued by the US Treasury.

scenes.head: How US TIPS work (US Treasury, checked October 2026)

segs.say: How US TIPS work (US Treasury, checked October 2026). The principal of a TIPS goes up with inflation and down with deflation, using the Consumer Price Index from the Bureau of Labor Statistics; Treasury’s TIPS data identify it as the non-seasonally adjusted CPI-U. TIPS pay interest every six months at a fixed rate, set at auction and never less than 0.125%, and each payment is the adjusted principal times half the annual rate, so the dollar amount of interest changes as the principal changes. At maturity the holder receives the adjusted principal or the original principal, whichever is greater. TIPS are sold in terms of 5, 10 and 30 years, in multiples of $100. Interest is subject to federal income tax each year but not to state or local income tax, and changes in the principal during the year may also affect federal tax.

scenes.head: A simplified illustration (fictional numbers; Treasury’s own calculation uses a daily index ratio): $10,000 of TIPS with a fixed rate of 1.75%.

segs.say: A simplified illustration (fictional numbers; Treasury’s own calculation uses a daily index ratio): $10,000 of TIPS with a fixed rate of 1.75%. If the index ratio is 1.015 at the first payment date, the adjusted principal is $10,150 and the payment is 10,150 × 0.0175 ÷ 2 ≈ 88.81 dollars. If the ratio reaches 1.032 a year in, the principal is $10,320 and the payment $90.30. If, at maturity, deflation had left the adjusted principal at $9,800, the holder would still receive $10,000.

scenes.head: Because a TIPS fixes a real rate and an ordinary Treasury of the same term fixes a nominal rate, comparing the two reveals the break-even inflation…

segs.say: Because a TIPS fixes a real rate and an ordinary Treasury of the same term fixes a nominal rate, comparing the two reveals the break-even inflation rate: (1 + nominal yield) ÷ (1 + real yield) − 1. If inflation turns out higher than break-even, the TIPS does better; if lower, the ordinary bond does. Worked example 3 makes the comparison.

scenes.head: Every real calculation about the future rests on an inflation forecast, and forecasts are uncertain.

segs.say: Every real calculation about the future rests on an inflation forecast, and forecasts are uncertain. A plan made at 2.8% looks different at 5%. Good practice is to state the assumption, test two or three alternatives, and prefer contracts or investments whose real value does not hinge on getting it exactly right. Past inflation, measured from an index, is a fact; future inflation is an assumption.

scenes.head: Cumulative and average annual inflation

segs.say: Cumulative and average annual inflation: Iₙ = CPIₙ/CPI₀ − 1, i_(avg) = (CPIₙ/CPI₀)^(1/n) − 1.
Iₙ: Cumulative inflation over the whole interval, as a decimal.
i_(avg): Average annual inflation rate: the constant yearly rate giving the same cumulative inflation (per year).
CPI₀: Price index at the start (index points).
CPIₙ: Price index at the end (index points).
n: Number of years in the interval (years).
It assumes this: Any price index can stand in for the CPI; use the same series at both dates.
Never divide cumulative inflation by n: inflation compounds.

scenes.head: Restating an amount in base-period dollars

segs.say: Restating an amount in base-period dollars: Real amount = Nominal amountₜ × (CPI_(base))/CPIₜ = (Nominal amountₜ)/(1 + i)ᵗ.
Nominal amountₜ: An amount paid or received at date t, in that date’s dollars ($).
CPIₜ: Price index at date t (index points).
CPI_(base): Price index at the base date (index points).
i: Constant annual inflation rate (the second form only, for forecasts) (per year).
t: Years from the base date to the payment (years).
Real amount: What the amount buys at base-date prices ($ of the base date).
It assumes this: The index (or the inflation rate) measures the price changes that matter to the person or business.
Multiply by CPI_t ÷ CPI_base to go the other way, from base-date dollars to date-t dollars.

scenes.head: Fisher relation (exact)

segs.say: Fisher relation (exact): 1 + rₙₒₘ = (1 + rᵣₑₐₗ)(1 + i) ⇔ rᵣₑₐₗ = (1 + rₙₒₘ)/(1 + i) − 1.
rₙₒₘ: Nominal rate: growth in dollars, as an effective rate for the period (per period).
rᵣₑₐₗ: Real rate: growth in purchasing power over the same period (per period).
i: Inflation over the same period (per period).
It assumes this: All three rates cover the same period and are effective rates (convert an APR to an EAR first).
The shortcut r_real ≈ r_nom − i drops the product r_real × i; use it only as a check.

scenes.head: Real and nominal cash flows

segs.say: Real and nominal cash flows: C^(nom)ₜ = C^(real)ₜ (1 + i)ᵗ.
C^(nom)ₜ: Cash flow in year t, in the dollars of year t ($).
C^(real)ₜ: The same cash flow in today’s dollars ($ of today).
i: Expected annual inflation (per year).
t: Years from today (years).
It assumes this: Inflation is expected to be constant at i; with a forecast that varies, multiply the yearly factors.

scenes.head: Consistent discounting

segs.say: Consistent discounting: PV = Σₜ₌₁ⁿ (C^(nom)ₜ)/(1 + rₙₒₘ)ᵗ = Σₜ₌₁ⁿ (C^(real)ₜ)/(1 + rᵣₑₐₗ)ᵗ.
PV: Present value today ($).
C^(nom)ₜ: Nominal cash flow at the end of year t ($).
C^(real)ₜ: Real cash flow at the end of year t, in today’s dollars ($ of today).
rₙₒₘ: Nominal discount rate (per year).
rᵣₑₐₗ: Real discount rate, linked to the nominal rate by the Fisher relation (per year).
n: Number of years (years).
t: Year of each cash flow (years).
It assumes this: The same inflation rate links the cash flows and the discount rates.
Never discount nominal flows at a real rate or real flows at a nominal rate.

scenes.head: Real growth of a salary or price

segs.say: Real growth of a salary or price: gᵣₑₐₗ = (1 + g)/(1 + i) − 1.
gᵣₑₐₗ: Growth in purchasing power per year (per year).
g: Nominal growth rate per year (for example a pay rise) (per year).
i: Inflation per year (per year).
The Fisher relation applied to growth instead of interest.

scenes.head: TIPS principal and interest (simplified)

segs.say: TIPS principal and interest (simplified): Adjusted principalₜ = Principal × CPIₜ/CPI₀, Interestₜ = Adjusted principalₜ × (r_(fixed))/2.
Principal: Original principal (par value) ($).
Adjusted principalₜ: Principal after the inflation adjustment at date t ($).
CPI₀: Reference price index when the security was issued (index points).
CPIₜ: Reference price index at payment date t (index points).
r_(fixed): Fixed annual interest rate set at auction (per year).
Interestₜ: Interest paid at the six-monthly payment date t ($).
It assumes this: Treasury uses a daily index ratio based on the CPI; the ratio CPI_t ÷ CPI_0 here stands in for it.
At maturity the holder receives the greater of the adjusted principal and the original principal.

chapters.title: Example: Five years of prices and a pay rise

scenes.head: Five years of prices and a pay rise

segs.say: Use the fictional index in “The idea” (100.0 in Year 0, 122.9 in Year 5). A technician’s salary rose from $45,000 in Year 0 to $52,000 in Year 5. Find (a) cumulative inflation, (b) the average annual inflation rate and (c) the Year 5 salary in Year 0 dollars, and say whether her purchasing power rose.

scenes.head: Five years of prices and a pay rise

segs.say: Step 1. (a) Cumulative inflation is the ratio of the index levels minus one: 122.9 ÷ 100.0 − 1 = 0.229, or 22.9%.
Step 2. (b) The average annual rate compounds backwards: 1.229^(1/5) − 1 ≈ 0.042102, about 4.21% a year. (On a calculator: 1.229, then the power key with 0.2.)
Step 3. (c) Restate the Year 5 salary at Year 0 prices: 52,000 × 100.0 ÷ 122.9 ≈ 42,310.82.
Step 4. Compare: in Year 0 dollars her salary went from $45,000 to $42,310.82, a real change of 42,310.82 ÷ 45,000 − 1 ≈ −5.98%, while in dollars it rose 52,000 ÷ 45,000 − 1 ≈ 15.56%.

scenes.head: Five years of prices and a pay rise

segs.say: (a) 22.9%; (b) about 4.21% a year; (c) about $42,310.82 in Year 0 dollars, so her purchasing power fell by about 5.98% despite a 15.56% rise in pay.
A pay rise is a real rise only if it beats inflation over the same period. To keep pace she needed $55,305 in Year 5. Comparing salaries across years in nominal dollars hides exactly this.

chapters.title: Example: Lantern’s catering contract, valued two ways

scenes.head: Lantern’s catering contract, valued two ways

segs.say: The law firm offers Lantern either $42,000 at the end of each of the next three years, or $40,000 in March 2027 dollars at the end of each year, raised in line with the CPI. Lantern requires a nominal return of 10% a year and expects inflation of 2.8% a year. Value the indexed offer by the nominal route and by the real route, value the fixed offer, and recommend one.

scenes.head: Lantern’s catering contract, valued two ways

segs.say: Step 3. Real route: the real rate is 1.10 ÷ 1.028 − 1 ≈ 7.0039%. The real fee is a level $40,000, so use the annuity factor at the real rate: 40,000 × (1 − 1.070039⁻³)/0.070039 ≈ 40,000 × 2.624129 ≈ 104,965.18. The same answer, as it must be.
Step 5. Compare: the indexed offer is worth about 104,965.18 − 104,447.78 = 517.40 dollars more. The fixed fee that would make Lantern indifferent is 104,965.18 ÷ 2.486852 ≈ 42,208.05 a year.

scenes.head: Lantern’s catering contract, valued two ways

segs.say: The indexed offer is worth about $104,965.18 today by either route; the fixed offer about $104,447.78. On a 2.8% inflation assumption Lantern should prefer the indexed fee, by about $517.40.

The margin is small, so the decision rests partly on risk. The indexed fee keeps its purchasing power whatever inflation does, which matters to a coffee caterer whose costs rise with prices; the fixed fee wins only if inflation turns out below about 2.54% a year. Lantern should also check which index the contract names and that it is not seasonally adjusted.

chapters.title: Example: An inflation-protected bond or an ordinary one?

scenes.head: An inflation-protected bond or an ordinary one?

segs.say: Tobias, a hospital pharmacist (fictional), is saving for a sabbatical in five years. He compares a five-year US Treasury note yielding 4.3% a year with five-year TIPS yielding a real 1.8% a year. Treat both yields as effective annual rates and ignore taxes. The yields are illustrations, not current market rates. What inflation rate makes the two equal, and what does each earn if inflation averages 3.5%, or 1.0%?

scenes.head: An inflation-protected bond or an ordinary one?

segs.say: Step 1. Break-even inflation from the Fisher relation: 1.043 ÷ 1.018 − 1 ≈ 2.456% a year (the subtraction shortcut says 2.5%).

Step 2. If inflation averages 3.5%: the TIPS earns 1.018 × 1.035 − 1 ≈ 5.363% nominal, more than the note’s 4.3%. The note’s real return is only 1.043 ÷ 1.035 − 1 ≈ 0.773%, against the TIPS’s fixed 1.8%.
Step 3. If inflation averages 1.0%: the TIPS earns 1.018 × 1.01 − 1 ≈ 2.818% nominal; the note still pays 4.3%, a real 1.043 ÷ 1.01 − 1 ≈ 3.267%.
Step 4. Judgement: the ordinary note wins if inflation stays below about 2.46% a year; the TIPS wins above it, and its real return is fixed at 1.8% either way.

scenes.head: An inflation-protected bond or an ordinary one?

segs.say: Break-even inflation is about 2.46% a year. At 3.5% inflation the TIPS earns about 5.36% nominal against 4.3%; at 1.0% it earns about 2.82% against 4.3%.

The choice is not about which bond has the higher number on it; it is about who carries inflation risk. Tobias’s sabbatical will be paid for in future prices, so locking in a real return removes a risk he cannot otherwise control. If he expects inflation well below 2.46%, or needs a predictable dollar sum, the ordinary note suits him better.

scenes.head: Discounting real and nominal cash flows

segs.say: Value a payment that keeps its purchasing power for several years. The two correct routes always agree; watch how far the two mixed-up routes drift from them as you lengthen the period or raise inflation. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: A salary in nominal and real terms

segs.say: A salary that rises by a fixed percentage each year, against steady inflation. Find the raise at which the real salary stops falling, and compare the exact real growth rate with the subtraction shortcut. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: What $1,000 received in a future year is worth today

segs.say: What $1,000 received in a future year is worth in today’s dollars at three steady inflation rates. Even 2% a year takes almost half of its purchasing power over thirty years. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Dividing cumulative inflation by the number of years

segs.say: Dividing cumulative inflation by the number of years. Prices that rose 22.9% over five years did not rise 4.58% a year: inflation compounds. The average annual rate is the fifth root of 1.229, minus one, about 4.21%.

scenes.head: Discounting real cash flows at a nominal rate

segs.say: Discounting real cash flows at a nominal rate. A forecast in today’s prices has no inflation in it; a nominal rate does. Lantern’s indexed fee discounted at 10% is undervalued by about $5,491. Convert the flows to nominal, or the rate to real, before discounting.

scenes.head: Discounting nominal cash flows at a real rate

segs.say: Discounting nominal cash flows at a real rate. The opposite mix counts inflation in the cash flows but not in the rate, and overvalues: about $5,850 too much for Lantern’s offer. Fixed loan payments, coupons and fixed-price contracts are nominal.

scenes.head: Putting an APR into the Fisher relation

segs.say: Putting an APR into the Fisher relation. The Fisher relation links effective rates over the same period. A 4.5% APR compounded monthly is an effective 4.594% a year; use that, or convert everything to monthly rates.

scenes.head: Calling a pay rise a real rise

segs.say: Calling a pay rise a real rise. A 3.5% raise with 2.8% inflation is a 0.68% real raise; with 4% inflation it is a real cut. Always ask what the increase is worth after prices.

scenes.head: Thinking a TIPS pays its fixed rate on the original principal

segs.say: Thinking a TIPS pays its fixed rate on the original principal. Interest is the adjusted principal times half the fixed annual rate, so the dollar amount of interest rises with inflation and falls with deflation. Only the final repayment has a floor: never less than the original principal.

scenes.head: Ana takes the indexed fee.

segs.say: Ana takes the indexed fee. Her own costs, beans, milk, rent and wages, rise with prices, so a fee that keeps its purchasing power is a better match for them, and on her 2.8% assumption it is also worth slightly more. Before signing she asks the law firm to name the index (the US City Average CPI, not seasonally adjusted, as the Bureau of Labor Statistics recommends for escalation) and the month used for each year’s adjustment. Lantern’s budget for the contract is prepared in March 2027 dollars and discounted at the real rate, so that her forecast of costs and the fee are measured the same way.

scenes.head: Budgeting in constant dollars.

segs.say: Budgeting in constant dollars. The facilities director of a fictional university plans roof and boiler replacements over twenty years. Contractors quote today’s prices, so she keeps the whole plan in real terms and discounts at a real rate. Converting to nominal would add an inflation forecast to every line without changing the answer, as long as the rate is converted the same way. When a contractor quotes a fixed nominal price for work three years away, she converts that single line to real terms before adding it in.

scenes.head: Pay negotiations.

segs.say: Pay negotiations. An HR manager at a fictional regional bus operator compares a union’s claim for a 5% rise with the company’s offer of 3% plus a cost-of-living adjustment linked to the CPI. She restates both offers in real terms under several inflation scenarios: at 2% inflation the fixed 5% is the better deal for staff; at 6% the indexed offer is. Escalation clauses of this kind, common in labour agreements, rental contracts and long supply contracts, move inflation risk from the payee to the payer.

scenes.head: Protecting savings.

segs.say: Protecting savings. A financial planner helping a fictional retired teacher compares ordinary Treasury securities with TIPS. She computes the break-even inflation rate from the two yields, explains that TIPS fix the real return while ordinary Treasuries fix the nominal one, and points out that the teacher’s pension is fixed in dollars, so some inflation protection elsewhere reduces her overall risk.

scenes.head: The same habit runs through all four: write down whether each number is nominal or real, keep one kind of dollar within a calculation, and state the…

segs.say: The same habit runs through all four: write down whether each number is nominal or real, keep one kind of dollar within a calculation, and state the inflation assumption so others can test it. The next lesson, Mortgages, applies this to the largest fixed nominal payment most households ever make.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: Nominal amounts are in the dollars of the date paid; real amounts are restated in the purchasing power of a base date. Convert with the ratio of index levels.
Inflation compounds: cumulative inflation = CPI_n ÷ CPI_0 − 1; average annual inflation = (CPI_n ÷ CPI_0)^(1/n) − 1, not cumulative ÷ n.
Fisher relation (exact): 1 + nominal = (1 + real)(1 + inflation), with effective rates over the same period.
Discount nominal cash flows at nominal rates and real cash flows at real rates; done consistently, both give the same present value. Lantern’s indexed fee is worth about $104,965.18 either way.
Mixing them is costly: real flows at a nominal rate undervalue, nominal flows at a real rate overvalue.
Real growth of a salary or price = (1 + nominal growth) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1.

US TIPS index their principal to the CPI, pay a fixed rate on the adjusted principal every six months, and repay at least the original principal; break-even inflation = (1 + nominal yield) ÷ (1 + real yield) − 1.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
